# Richard Stallman – Summary
Richard Stallman, born in 1953 in New York City, is a prominent figure in computer programming and digital activism. He attended Harvard, excelling in mathematics and physics, and became a programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1971 where he contributed to the development of projects like TECO and Emacs and was a strong proponent of the hacker community's free access philosophy. Stallman became concerned about proprietary software restrictions in the late 1970s and early 1980s, leading him to champion the rights of users to access, share, and modify software. In 1984, he left MIT to launch the GNU project, aiming to create a free Unix-compatible operating system, and later founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF). He popularized copyleft through the GNU General Public License and was responsible for tools such as GNU Emacs, GCC, and GNU Debugger.
Stallman has been central to the free software movement, advocating for software freedom and user rights, and is known for strong positions on terminology (e.g., preferring “free software” over “open source” and “GNU/Linux” for Linux systems using GNU components). His activism extends to copyright reform, anti-surveillance stances, and opposition to proprietary software and DRM. Stallman resigned from the FSF and MIT in 2019 following controversy over comments related to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal but returned to the FSF board in 2021. He has received numerous honors for his contributions, including the MacArthur Fellowship and membership in the US National Academy of Engineering, and remains a key figure in free software advocacy.
